scenes.name: a model is a file of numbers
scenes.visual: Dark canvas, one continuous shot that starts on a single object and then pulls back to show its scale. Centre: a file icon (Phosphor 'file', blue outline) that opens into a grid of forty blue rounded number tiles, 10 columns by 4 rows. The top row begins 0.13, −0.7, 0.02, 1.44, −0.3; the other 35 tiles hold varied values between about −1 and +1.5 (for example 0.41, −0.05, 0.88, −0.92, 0.27), never a visible repeating pattern. These five first-row values are reused in scenes 4 and 5, so keep them exact. The grid is the anchor of the scene; a number line below it and a counter in the top-right come and go around it. Colour: blue for stored numbers, white and grey for text. No amber or coral yet, because nothing is computed or moved in this scene.

beats.say: Let's start from absolute zero. When people say a company has trained a model, what they actually have at the end of it is a file.
beats.show: Centre: the file icon fades up alone on the dark canvas, label beneath it 'a trained model'. It holds still on 'a file'.

beats.say: Open it, and here is everything inside. No rules. No instructions. No text. Just numbers. Point one three. Minus point seven. Point zero two. One point four four. Minus point three.
beats.show: On 'open it', the file icon unfolds and the 40-tile grid cascades out row by row to fill the centre. On 'no rules', 'no instructions', 'no text', three grey words appear in a column at the left, 'rules', 'instructions', 'text', and a strike-through line draws across each as it is spoken. On the five spoken numbers, the first five tiles of the top row pulse in turn: 0.13, −0.7, 0.02, 1.44, −0.3.

beats.say: Each number sits somewhere between about minus one and plus one. Forty are drawn here. A large model has seventy billion of them, one after another in a single, very long list.
beats.show: A short number line from −1 to +1 draws under the grid; each tile drops a dot onto it and the dots cluster inside that range (1.44 lands just past the right end, which is why the narration says 'about'). On 'forty', a small label '40 shown' appears beside the grid. On 'seventy billion', the camera pulls back fast: the grid shrinks to a speck inside a field of tiles that fills the frame, and a counter in the top-right runs from 40 to 70,000,000,000, labelled 'numbers in one model'.

beats.say: How many is seventy billion? If you read one number aloud every second, day and night, without ever stopping, you would finish in about two thousand two hundred years.
beats.show: The tile field dims. Left third: a stopwatch icon ticking once per second. Right third: a year counter running up to '≈ 2,218 years' as the sentence ends, with a small grey line under it, '1 number per second, non-stop'. The '70,000,000,000' counter stays top-right.

beats.say: Each of these numbers is called a parameter, or a weight. The two words mean exactly the same thing, and you will hear both.
beats.show: The camera pushes back in to the 40-tile grid. The tile holding 1.44 lifts out and enlarges at centre. On 'parameter', the word 'parameter' slides in to its left; on 'weight', the word 'weight' slides in to its right, with an '=' sign between the two words.

beats.say: It is worth starting here, because everything that follows is arithmetic on this list. Training produced the numbers. Inference is the business of using them, and inference is what this whole film is about.
beats.show: The 1.44 tile drops back into the grid. Under the grid, two short labels appear side by side: left 'training: produced them' in grey, right 'inference: uses them' in blue. The right one brightens with a soft glow on 'what this whole film is about'. Bottom band: 'everything later is arithmetic on this list'.

scenes.name: the two lives of a model
scenes.visual: Two tall panels side by side, left 'Training' and right 'Inference', with an arrow running from left to right between them. The 40-tile grid from scene 1, shrunk small, rides along that arrow: what training outputs is exactly what inference uses. Each panel fills with three facts, each an icon plus two or three words, landing as they are spoken. By the end the training panel is greyed out as finished and the inference panel is lit in blue, as the one the film lives in.

beats.say: A model lives two very different lives. The first is training. Training is the search for those seventy billion numbers. It reads an enormous amount of text, and keeps adjusting the numbers until the model predicts well.
beats.show: The left panel draws on, title 'Training'. Inside it, a stack of document icons streams into the small tile grid, and the tile values flicker and change as the text flows in.

beats.say: Training takes months. It runs on thousands of chips at once. And it is done once.
beats.show: Three facts land in the left panel, one per phrase: a calendar icon with 'months', a dense block of small chip icons with 'thousands of chips', and a stamp '1×' with 'done once'.

beats.say: The second life is inference, which simply means using the numbers. Once training ends, they never change again. Every answer the model will ever give comes from the same fixed list.
beats.show: The arrow draws from the left panel to the right, carrying the small tile grid across. On 'never change again', a padlock icon snaps shut on the grid and the tiles stop flickering; small tag 'fixed'. The right panel draws on, title 'Inference', with the locked grid at its top.

beats.say: Inference takes milliseconds. It runs on one chip, or a few. And it happens every single time anyone, anywhere, asks the model anything.
beats.show: Three facts land in the right panel: a stopwatch icon with 'milliseconds', one or two chip icons with 'one chip or a few', and a short row of user icons, each popping a small chat bubble in turn, with 'every time anyone asks'. The user icons keep popping bubbles on a loop.

beats.say: Everything in this film is about the second box. The first is finished before we begin. Keep the two apart, because almost every confusing claim about the cost or speed of these models turns out to be about the wrong one.
beats.show: The training panel dims to grey and gets a small tag 'finished'; the inference panel brightens blue and scales up slightly. Bottom band: 'cost or speed? check which phase'.

scenes.name: how the numbers were found
scenes.visual: A three-station cycle at centre, drawn as a circle that really runs: station 1 at the top 'guess the next word', station 2 at lower right 'compare with the real one', station 3 at lower left 'nudge every weight', with arrows running clockwise round the circle. The small tile grid sits in the middle of the circle. Top band: a sample sentence with its last word hidden. A grey corner tag 'training, briefly' stays all scene, because the film never trains anything. The cycle speeds up until it blurs, then collapses back into the file icon from scene 1.

beats.say: So where did the numbers come from? We will keep this brief, because nothing in this film ever trains anything. But the word trained should not stay a black box. It comes down to three steps.
beats.show: Centre: the small tile grid. Around it a circle draws on with three empty station markers. Top-left corner tag: 'training, briefly'.

beats.say: Step one. Take some real text, hide the word that comes next, and let the model guess it.
beats.show: Top band: blue pills 'the cat sat on the' followed by a dashed blank slot. Station 1 lights up: 'guess the next word'. A guess pill 'sofa' pops into the blank.

beats.say: Step two. Compare the guess with the word that really came next. Here the model said sofa, and the real word was mat.
beats.show: Station 2 lights up: 'compare with the real one'. The true word 'mat' appears under the blank; 'sofa' and 'mat' sit side by side and a small grey gap marker draws between them, labelled 'off by this much'.

beats.say: Step three. Nudge every single weight by a tiny amount, in whichever direction would have made that guess a little better. Then repeat, over an enormous amount of text.
beats.show: Station 3 lights up: 'nudge every weight'. Every tile in the centre grid changes in its last digit at the same moment, for example 0.13 becomes 0.131 and −0.7 becomes −0.699. On 'repeat', the cycle starts running: a dot travels round the three stations, the top-band sentence swaps to a new sentence on each lap, and the laps speed up. Label under the circle: 'repeat, over an enormous amount of text'.

beats.say: Each nudge is tiny, and there are trillions of them. Nobody chooses the values by hand. And nobody can look at one weight and say what it is for.
beats.show: The cycle blurs into a spinning ring. A counter labelled 'nudges' runs up into the trillions. Then the ring slows, one tile is plucked out of the grid and enlarged, and a large grey question mark appears beside it with 'what is it for?' underneath.

beats.say: What comes out is a file of numbers that happens to predict text very well. That is the whole of what a trained model is.
beats.show: The cycle stops and fades. The plucked tile drops back, and the grid compacts and folds back into the file icon from scene 1, label 'a trained model'.

scenes.name: one weight is a dial
scenes.visual: An equation row across the upper centre: a blue box 'input', an amber '×', the weight as a blue tile, an amber '=', and an amber-outlined box 'contribution'. The weight tile then becomes a rotary dial with a pointer, its scale marked from −1 to +1.5 with 0 at the top. Below the equation, a horizontal axis with a zero tick at its centre shows the contribution: an amber bar grows right for positive, left for negative. The input stays at 2 for all three dial settings so that only the dial changes. The settings 1.44 and −0.7 are numbers from the file in scene 1; 0 is the 'off' position. Amber here because this is arithmetic.

beats.say: So what does a single weight actually do? It takes part in one multiplication. A number comes in, it is multiplied by the weight, and the result is that number's contribution.
beats.show: The equation builds term by term as the words land: the blue 'input' box on 'a number comes in', amber '×', the weight tile on 'multiplied by the weight', amber '=', and the amber 'contribution' box on 'contribution'.

beats.say: Think of the weight as a dial. It decides how much one number gets to influence the next one.
beats.show: The weight tile morphs into the rotary dial with its scale. Under the equation, the horizontal contribution axis draws on with a '0' tick at its centre.

beats.say: Let's turn it. Say the input is two. Set the dial to zero, and two times zero is zero. The input is ignored entirely.
beats.show: '2' fills the input box. The dial swings to 0. The contribution box reads '0', the bar stays a dot at zero, and the input box greys out. Tag beside the bar: 'ignored'.

beats.say: Now turn it up to one point four four, one of the numbers from our file. Two times one point four four is two point eight eight. This input now dominates.
beats.show: The dial swings to 1.44. The contribution box counts up to '2.88' and the amber bar grows long to the right. The input box brightens. Tag: 'dominates'.

beats.say: Turn it negative, to minus point seven. Two times minus point seven is minus one point four. Now the input pushes the other way.
beats.show: The dial swings back past zero to −0.7. The contribution box reads '−1.4' and the amber bar sweeps through zero and grows to the left. Tag: 'pushes the other way'.

beats.say: That is the whole of what one weight does. Training was the search for seventy billion settings of these dials that make the output text useful.
beats.show: The equation holds in front. Behind it, the single dial duplicates, then multiplies into a faint wall of thousands of tiny dials filling the background, each at a different angle. Top-right counter: '70,000,000,000 dials'.

beats.say: So the intelligence is not in any one dial. It lives in how seventy billion of them combine.
beats.show: One dial in the wall turns on its own and nothing else visibly changes; then a wave of turning sweeps across the whole wall at once. Bottom band: 'not one dial: how they combine'.

scenes.name: multiply, then add
scenes.visual: Left half: five rows stacked top to bottom, each a blue input box, an amber '×', and a blue weight tile. Inputs are 2, 1, 5, 1, 1 (made up for the example); weights are the first five numbers from the file, 0.13, −0.7, 0.02, 1.44, −0.3. From each row an arrow converges on one amber box at centre-right, 'add them up', which feeds a final box at the right edge, 'one output'. Products travel as small amber chips along the arrows. Later the whole diagram shrinks into a cell that tiles into a sheet and stacks into a tower, then returns.

beats.say: Here is how they combine. Take five inputs. Give each one its own weight, here the first five numbers from our file. Then multiply each pair.
beats.show: The five rows build top to bottom: input boxes 2, 1, 5, 1, 1, each followed by '×' and its weight tile 0.13, −0.7, 0.02, 1.44, −0.3. On 'multiply each pair', each row flashes amber in turn and produces a product chip at its right end: 0.26, −0.7, 0.1, 1.44, −0.3.

beats.say: Now add the five results together. Point two six, minus point seven, point one, one point four four, and minus point three. Together they make point eight. One output value.
beats.show: The five chips slide along the converging arrows into the 'add them up' box, one per spoken number, and a running total inside the box ticks 0.26, −0.44, −0.34, 1.10, 0.80. On 'one output value', the box emits '0.8' into the 'one output' box at the right.

beats.say: Multiply each input by its own weight, then add up the results. That is the only arithmetic pattern a model performs. There is nothing else in there.
beats.show: Bottom band, amber: 'multiply, then add'. The whole diagram pulses once, left to right, following the flow from inputs to output.

beats.say: A model is built as a tall stack of stages called layers. We will open one up later. For now, just know this: every layer of every large language model is this same pattern, repeated at enormous scale.
beats.show: The five-row diagram shrinks into one small cell. The cell tiles into a wide sheet of hundreds of identical cells, and the sheet stacks upward into a tall tower of thin slabs, labelled 'layers'. Small grey tag: 'opened up later'.

beats.say: Notice the bookkeeping, too. Every weight was used exactly once: one multiplication, then one addition into the total. Hold on to this picture. When we later count how much work a model does, this is exactly what we will be counting.
beats.show: The tower collapses back into the five-row diagram. Beside each weight tile, a small amber pair '×' and '+' ticks on, top to bottom, five pairs in all. The bottom band changes to: 'each weight: one multiply, one add'.

scenes.name: text becomes tokens
scenes.visual: Top band: a long blue-outlined sentence bar reading 'the quick brown fox jumps', which is cut into five blue token pills. Right third: a second example, a rarer word splitting into pieces. Bottom band: two bars drawn to the same scale comparing a count of words with a count of tokens. Finally three unit cards stack at the right. Blue throughout: tokens are the film's basic unit of structure.

beats.say: So far, the inputs have just been numbers. But we talk to a model in text. So before anything else happens, the text is cut into pieces, called tokens.
beats.show: A chat bubble icon at the left; its text flies out into a sentence bar across the top: 'the quick brown fox jumps'. On 'cut into pieces', small scissor marks snip between the words and the bar breaks into five blue pills: 'the', 'quick', 'brown', 'fox', 'jumps'. On 'tokens', a label appears under them: 'five tokens'.

beats.say: Here, each word became exactly one token. Five words, five tokens. Common words usually are a single token. Rarer words get split into two or three pieces.
beats.show: The five pills pulse one after another with a small counter running 1 to 5. Right third: a rarer word 'unbelievably' appears in a bar and splits into three pills, 'un', 'believ', 'ably'. Grey tag under it: 'illustrative split'.

beats.say: So a token is roughly a word, but not exactly. As a rule of thumb, five hundred words of English come to about six to eight hundred tokens.
beats.show: Bottom band, two horizontal bars on the same scale: a blue bar '500 words', and below it a token bar whose end is a shaded range from 600 to 800, labelled 'about 600–800 tokens'. Small grey note at the right: '1.2 to 1.6 tokens per word'.

beats.say: The model never sees letters. It works only in these pieces, and it produces them one at a time. How a piece of text becomes numbers the model can multiply is a story for later.
beats.show: The letters inside the five top pills blur away, leaving plain blue pills: the model's-eye view. On 'one at a time', a sixth pill pops in at the right end on its own. Grey tag: 'text to numbers: later'.

beats.say: Tokens are the unit everything is counted in from now on. Tokens per second. Cost per token. Milliseconds per token.
beats.show: Three cards stack at the right, one per phrase, each with a small token-pill icon: 'tokens per second', 'cost per token', 'milliseconds per token'.

beats.say: And one small refinement to earlier. When training guessed the next word, strictly speaking, it was guessing the next token.
beats.show: A small inset of the training sentence from scene 3, 'the cat sat on the ___', slides in at the bottom-left with its station label 'guess the next word'; the word 'word' is struck through and replaced by 'token'.

scenes.name: the generate loop
scenes.visual: A large rounded panel fills the centre, titled 'One turn of the loop'. Inside, left to right: a blue box 'text so far' holding a row of token pills, an arrow, a coral box 'run the whole model' with the small tile grid inside it, an arrow, and a box 'one new token'. A return arrow runs from 'one new token' down and back along the bottom to 'text so far', labelled 'append it, go round again'. Coral marks the expensive step. The loop physically runs: on each turn the pills pass through the coral box and every tile in it lights up. A counter in the top-right: 'runs of the whole model'.

beats.say: One at a time is meant literally. A model does not write a sentence. Here is a single turn of what is called the generate loop. The text so far goes in. The whole model runs. One new token comes out.
beats.show: The panel draws on with its title. The pills 'the quick brown fox jumps' sit in 'text so far'. On 'the whole model runs', copies of the pills flow into the coral box and its tile grid lights up top to bottom, every tile. On 'one new token', a blue pill 'over' pops into the third box. Counter top-right: '1'.

beats.say: That token is added to the end of the text. Then the entire model runs again, from the start, to predict the next one. And again. And again.
beats.show: 'over' travels along the return arrow and appends to the pill row. The loop turns three more times, each a little faster, appending 'the', 'lazy', 'dog'. On every turn the coral box lights up fully, every tile, top to bottom. Counter: 2, 3, 4.

beats.say: So how many runs does a whole answer take? A two-hundred-word answer, at roughly one and a half tokens per word, is about three hundred tokens.
beats.show: Bottom band, an equation builds term by term: '200 words' × '~1.5 tokens per word' = '≈ 300 tokens'. Small grey note beneath: 'at 1.2–1.6 per word: 240–320'.

beats.say: That means running the entire seventy-billion-parameter model about three hundred times. Once per token.
beats.show: The loop speeds into a blur and the counter runs to 300. A label on the coral box adds: '70 billion weights, every turn'.

beats.say: This loop is the shape of the entire problem. Almost everything difficult about inference follows from one fact: the whole model has to be repeated for every single token.
beats.show: The loop slows and holds on one turn; the return arrow glows. The bottom band replaces the equation with: 'the whole model, once per token'.

scenes.name: a score for every token
scenes.visual: Top band: the text so far as blue pills, 'curled up asleep on the sofa was a', then a dashed empty slot '?'. Below: a horizontal bar chart in amber, one row per candidate, label at the left with an icon (cat, dog and banana from Fluent Emoji Flat; 'the' as plain text), bar length drawn to scale of the score, the score value at the bar's end. The chart then extends into a long tail of tiny bars and re-forms as a sorted histogram. The scores are illustrative; the shape of the distribution is the point.

beats.say: Let's zoom into the end of one turn. What exactly comes out of the model? Not a word. Suppose the text so far reads, curled up asleep on the sofa was a. What comes next?
beats.show: The camera pushes into the 'one new token' box of the loop and through it into a new space. Top band: pills 'curled up asleep on the sofa was a' and a dashed slot '?' that blinks.

beats.say: The model scores every token it knows. Cat, eight point two. Dog, seven point one. The little word the, three point five. And banana, a poor fit, point four.
beats.show: Heading fades in: 'It scores every token it knows'. Four amber bars grow left to right, one as each is spoken, lengths to scale: cat (cat icon) 8.2, dog (dog icon) 7.1, 'the' 3.5, banana (banana icon) 0.4. Values appear at the bar ends.

beats.say: And it does not stop at four. The model's vocabulary, its full list of tokens, is about a hundred and twenty-eight thousand long, and every single one gets a score. Higher means a better fit.
beats.show: Under the four bars, a line 'and 128,252 more, all scored' appears with its number counting up; the chart extends downward and a dense column of tiny bars scrolls past fast. Small grey label in the corner: 'vocabulary: 128,256 tokens'.

beats.say: These raw numbers are called scores, or logits. The exact values here are illustrative, but the shape is real. One or two candidates stand out, and the rest trail off to nothing.
beats.show: The chart re-forms as a vertical histogram sorted from high to low: two tall bars at the left (cat, dog), a steep drop, then a long flat tail running off the right edge. Label: 'logits: the raw scores'. Grey tag: 'values illustrative, shape real'.

beats.say: Which clears up the most common misconception about language models: that they pick a word. They do not. They produce about a hundred and twenty-eight thousand numbers, and something else does the picking.
beats.show: Centre: the phrase 'the model picks a word' appears and is struck through. Under it, two lines: '128,000 scores out' and 'something else picks'. The dashed '?' slot in the top band stays empty.

scenes.name: softmax: scores become shares
scenes.visual: A four-row table at centre: rows cat, dog, the, banana; columns 'score', 'e to the score', 'share', and to the right of the share column an amber bar per row drawn to scale of its share (cat about three quarters of the full width, dog about a quarter, the and banana as slivers). Top band: a recipe card, 'e to each score, then divide by the total'. A total line sits under the second column. The input scores are illustrative but every number computed from them is real arithmetic. Only these four candidates are used, for clarity.

beats.say: Raw scores are awkward. Is eight point two a lot? What we want are shares of one whole, like slices of a pie that add up to a hundred percent. There is a standard two-step recipe for that.
beats.show: The four bars from the previous scene slide left and collapse into the 'score' column: 8.2, 7.1, 3.5, 0.4. On 'two-step recipe', the top-band card appears: 'e to each score, then divide by the total'.

beats.say: Step one. Take the number e, which is about two point seven one eight, and raise it to the power of each score. E to the eight point two is about three thousand six hundred and forty-one.
beats.show: A small card 'e ≈ 2.718' pops up beside the recipe. In the cat row, the 8.2 lifts up into a superscript over an 'e' and the cell resolves to '3,641'.

beats.say: E to the seven point one is about one thousand two hundred and twelve. For the word the, about thirty-three. And for banana, about one and a half.
beats.show: The same lift-and-resolve happens in each row as it is spoken: dog '1,212', the '33', banana '1.5'.

beats.say: Notice that every result is positive. E raised to any power is positive, so even a negative score would still give a positive value, just a small one.
beats.show: A small side note at the right: 'always positive', with an example 'e^−1 ≈ 0.37' that fades in and out. The four values in the column glow briefly.

beats.say: Step two. Add the four values up. That gives about four thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight. Then divide each value by that total.
beats.show: A sum line draws under the second column: 'total ≈ 4,888'. On 'divide', four short arrows run from the values into the empty 'share' column.

beats.say: Cat gets seventy-four point five percent. Dog, twenty-four point eight. The word the, zero point six eight percent. Banana, zero point zero three percent. To keep the arithmetic visible, we have treated these four as the only candidates.
beats.show: The share column fills row by row: 74.5%, 24.8%, 0.68%, 0.03%, and each row's amber share bar grows to scale as its number lands. Grey footnote at the bottom: 'four candidates only, for clarity'.

beats.say: The four shares add up to exactly one whole. This step is called softmax, and it is the reason a model's output is described as a probability.
beats.show: The four share bars slide end to end into one full-width bar with '= 1.00' at its right. On 'softmax', the label 'softmax' appears above the recipe card, which now reads as its definition.

beats.say: Now look at what the exponential did. Cat and dog differ in score by only about one, one point one to be exact. Yet cat ends up three times as likely as dog, seventy-four percent against twenty-five.
beats.show: A bracket joins the cat and dog score cells, labelled 'gap 1.1'. A second bracket joins their share cells, labelled '×3.0'. The cat and dog share bars brighten.

beats.say: And the little word the, four point seven behind cat, ends up a hundred and ten times less likely. Small differences in score become large differences in confidence. The exponential exaggerates every gap.
beats.show: A bracket joins the cat and 'the' score cells, 'gap 4.7', and a second joins their share cells, '×110'. Bottom band: 'the exponential exaggerates every gap'.

scenes.name: the draw: sampling
scenes.visual: Left third: the two leading share bars from scene 9, 'cat, 74.5%' and 'dog, 24.8%'. Centre-right: a spinner wheel with a fixed pointer at the top, its slices drawn to scale: cat 268 degrees, dog 89 degrees, the 2.4 degrees, banana 0.1 degrees (a hairline). Top band: the text 'curled up asleep on the sofa was a' with its empty slot; later it forks into two branches. Amber for the shares, blue for token pills. The scene ends on a recap strip of the whole chapter and a stopwatch with a question mark, handing over to the next chapter.

beats.say: So who does the picking? Not the model. The model hands over the same list every time it sees this text. Cat, seventy-four point five percent. Dog, twenty-four point eight.
beats.show: Left third: the two amber bars 'cat, 74.5%' and 'dog, 24.8%' slide in, with a label above them: 'same list, every time'. Top band: the sentence with its empty slot.

beats.say: The pick is a random draw, made in proportion to those shares. Picture a spinner with slices sized to match exactly. Making this draw is called sampling.
beats.show: The bars bend round into the spinner wheel at centre-right: the cat slice three quarters of the wheel, the dog slice a quarter, two thin slivers for the and banana. The pointer draws on at the top. Label under the wheel: 'sampling'.

beats.say: Spin once, and cat is likely. Spin again, and dog can win. About one time in four, it will.
beats.show: Spin 1: the wheel spins and stops on cat; a 'cat' pill drops into the slot. The slot clears. Spin 2: it stops on dog; 'dog' drops in. Then a quick run of many spins, with a tally beside the wheel climbing to roughly 'cat 75 · dog 25' out of 100 (an illustrative tally).

beats.say: And once dog has been drawn, it is appended to the text, and every later token is predicted from that new starting point. The answer takes a different turn from there on.
beats.show: The top-band sentence forks into two branches. Upper branch: '…was a cat', then pills 'purring' and 'softly' append one at a time. Lower branch: '…was a dog', then 'snoring' and 'loudly'. Each branch grows token by token, as if the loop is turning on each.

beats.say: That is why the same question can give different answers, and why nothing about the model itself has changed when it does. The difference lives entirely in that last step, the draw, not in the model.
beats.show: The locked file icon from scene 2 appears centred above both branches, unchanged, padlock closed. A highlight ring circles the spinner. Bottom band: 'same model, same list, different draw'.

beats.say: So here is the whole machine so far. A fixed file of seventy billion numbers. Text cut into tokens. The whole model run once per token, multiplying and adding, ending in scores, softmax, and a draw. Then round again.
beats.show: A recap strip assembles left to right across the centre, one element per phrase: the file icon '70 billion weights', a row of token pills 'tokens', the coral box 'whole model, per token', amber bars 'scores', the spinner 'draw', and an arrow curving back to the start.

beats.say: Which leaves one question. How long does a single turn of that loop take?
beats.show: The recap strip holds; a stopwatch icon fades in over the curved return arrow, with a '?' beside it. Hold for a beat.

checks.claim: Reading seventy billion numbers at one per second takes about 2,218 years
